title: Deciding pattern avoidance over a prescribed alphabet
formal: Is the following set decidable: pairs (p,k), where p is a nonempty finite word of variables and k≥2, such that there exists an infinite word \(w\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^{\mathbb N}\) containing no nonerasing substitution instance of p as a contiguous factor?
definitions:
The input pattern is an explicitly written finite sequence of variable identifiers; only equality of identifiers matters. The integer k is encoded in binary. A nonerasing substitution maps every variable occurring in p to a nonempty finite word over the k-letter alphabet and extends to p by concatenation. Repeated occurrences of a variable receive the same word; different variables may receive the same word. A forbidden occurrence is an interval of consecutive positions in w whose word equals h(p) for some such substitution h. The infinite word is one-sided, indexed by the nonnegative integers, with no computability, morphic-generation or eventual-periodicity requirement. It may use fewer than k symbols.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite pair and answers yes exactly when such an infinite avoiding word exists. No running-time bound is imposed. The question fixes the available alphabet size as part of the instance; testing whether some unspecified finite alphabet permits avoidance is a different decision problem. Partial words with holes and abelian pattern occurrences are also outside this target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked total decision procedure with equivalence to the stated infinite-word existence property, or a complete undecidability reduction whose outputs are valid pairs of the specified kind. A procedure that decides only avoidability over some finite alphabet, or verifies one proposed infinite construction, is insufficient.
context:
Blanchet-Sadri and Lohr distinguish general avoidability from avoidance on a prescribed number of letters. Their introduction identifies the latter decision question separately.

The paper also studies depth and partial words. Those results must not be confused with a decision procedure for the total-word question retained here.
why: This distinguishes decidability with a prescribed alphabet from the easier unrestricted-alphabet existence question.

import_provenance.original_title: Deciding pattern avoidance over a prescribed alphabet
import_provenance.original_statement: Given a finite pattern p whose symbols are variables and an integer k≥2, is there an algorithm deciding whether some infinite k-letter word avoids every nonerasing substitution instance of p? Decidability when the alphabet size is unrestricted is known; fixing its size is the unresolved issue explicitly discussed in Blanchet-Sadri’s pattern research.

sentences: A pattern identifies blocks that must repeat consistently.
An occurrence substitutes a nonempty word for each variable.
The question asks whether an infinite word over a prescribed finite alphabet can avoid every occurrence.
The desired algorithm must halt on all pattern and alphabet-size inputs.
Known questions about depth or unrestricted alphabet size are not the same decision problem.
